lessons.title: Culturing microorganisms
lessons.text:
## Culturing microorganisms
LV: GCSE
S: Scientists grow bacteria in the lab to test which substances kill them, but a culture is only useful if it contains just the microbe being studied. Knowing how bacteria multiply, and why each step of aseptic technique matters, lets you grow a pure culture safely.
O: Describe how bacteria multiply by binary fission and what affects how quickly they divide
O: Explain why tests of disinfectants, antiseptics and antibiotics need cultures free from contamination
O: Give a reason for each step used to prepare, inoculate and incubate an agar plate safely
REQ: aqa-gcse-biology:4.1.1.6.a @1
REQ: aqa-gcse-biology:4.1.1.6.c @2
REQ: aqa-gcse-biology:4.1.1.6.e @3
T: Binary fission | The simple cell division in which a bacterium copies its DNA and splits into two cells
T: Culture medium | A nutrient broth or agar gel that supplies what microorganisms need to grow
T: Aseptic technique | Laboratory methods that stop unwanted microorganisms contaminating a pure culture
T: Colony | A visible spot on agar made of many bacteria that grew from one original cell
H: How bacteria multiply
P: Bacteria reproduce by **binary fission**. The cell copies its DNA, then divides into two cells. Each of those can divide again, so the number keeps doubling.
P: The speed depends on conditions. With plenty of nutrients and a suitable temperature, one division can take as little as about 20 minutes. With fewer nutrients, or a temperature that does not suit them, division is much slower.
DNEED: One bacterial cell copying its DNA and splitting into two, then those two splitting into four, labelled "binary fission"
!: Thinking bacteria always divide every 20 minutes. About 20 minutes is the fastest case, and only when nutrients are plentiful and the temperature suits them.
H: Growing a culture
P: Microorganisms can be grown in a liquid **nutrient broth** or as colonies on a layer of set **agar gel** in a Petri dish. The medium supplies carbohydrate as an energy source, nitrogen so the cells can make protein, and minerals.
P: To make a plate, molten agar is poured into a sterile Petri dish and left to set. Bacteria are then spread over the surface. Spreading them thinly gives separate colonies; a sterile spreader can cover the whole surface to give an even "lawn" of bacteria.
H: Why the culture must be pure
P: When you test how well a disinfectant, antiseptic or antibiotic works, you need to know which microbe it is acting on. Stray microbes that get in compete with the test bacteria for nutrients, and some might be pathogens that cause disease. Either way the result no longer tells you about the bacterium you meant to test.
K: An uncontaminated culture is needed so that any effect you measure is caused by the substance acting on the one microbe being studied, and so that no dangerous microbes are grown by accident.
H: Aseptic technique, step by step
- **Sterilise the Petri dish and agar before use**, in an autoclave, or use dishes bought pre-sterilised. This kills any microbes already present.
- **Pass the inoculating loop through a Bunsen flame** before you use it to transfer bacteria. The heat kills microbes on the loop, so only the intended bacteria reach the agar.
- **Tape the lid on and label the plate**, but do not seal it all the way round. The tape stops microbes from the air getting in; leaving gaps lets oxygen in, so harmful anaerobic bacteria are not encouraged.
- **Store the plate upside down.** Condensation then cannot drip onto the agar and spread the culture, and airborne microbes are less likely to settle on it.
- **Incubate at no more than 25 °C in a school.** This lowers the chance of growing pathogens that thrive at human body temperature. Hospital laboratories use 37 °C because cultures grow faster there.
DNEED: A sequence showing a sterile Petri dish, a loop being heated in a Bunsen flame, a lid taped at a few points, the plate stored upside down and an incubator set to 25 °C, each with its reason
X: A student says, "I'll tape the lid all the way round so nothing can get in." Explain what is wrong.
> Tape on the lid is right: it stops microbes from the air contaminating the culture.
> Sealing it completely stops oxygen reaching the culture.
> Without oxygen, anaerobic bacteria, which include harmful types, are favoured.
> So the lid should be secured with a few pieces of tape, not sealed fully.
!: Thinking a fully sealed lid is the safest choice. The lid is secured but not sealed, so oxygen can enter and anaerobic pathogens are not encouraged.
!: Thinking 25 °C is used because bacteria grow best there. It is chosen to reduce the risk of growing human pathogens; many bacteria grow faster at 37 °C.
SAFE: Treat every culture as if it could contain pathogens: follow your teacher's instructions, never open a taped plate, and hand plates back for safe disposal.
Q: How do bacteria reproduce? | By binary fission: the cell copies its DNA and splits into two cells.
Q: What two things must be right for bacteria to divide as fast as about every 20 minutes? | Enough nutrients and a suitable temperature.
Q: Why is an inoculating loop passed through a flame before use? | The heat kills microbes on the loop, so only the intended bacteria are transferred.
Q: Why are agar plates stored upside down? | So condensation does not drip onto the agar and microbes from the air are less likely to settle on it.
Q: Why do school labs incubate cultures at 25 °C or below? | To reduce the chance of growing pathogens that grow well at human body temperature.
Q: Why must a culture be uncontaminated when testing an antibiotic? | Other microbes would compete for nutrients and could be pathogens, so the result would not show the antibiotic's effect on the test bacterium.
M1@1: By what process do bacteria multiply? | Binary fission, splitting into two cells | Meiosis, forming four sex cells | Budding off small spores from fungi | Fertilisation between two parent cells | Bacteria copy their DNA and divide into two cells, a simple division called binary fission.
M1@3: Why are Petri dishes and agar sterilised before a culture is grown? | To kill microbes already present on them | To add nutrients the bacteria need | To help the agar set more quickly | To make the bacteria divide faster | Sterilising kills any microbes already there, so only the bacteria you add will grow.
M2@2: A student tests an antibiotic on a plate that was contaminated by microbes from the air. Why is the result unreliable? | Other microbes compete for nutrients and might be pathogens | The antibiotic only works on plates kept at 37 °C | Contamination makes the agar melt before it is tested | Airborne microbes always make every antibiotic stronger | Contaminating microbes compete with the test bacteria and could cause disease, so the result no longer shows the antibiotic's effect on one microbe.
M2@1: In which conditions would a bacterial culture divide most quickly? | Plenty of nutrients at a suitable temperature | Few nutrients at a suitable temperature | Plenty of nutrients in a freezer | Few nutrients with the lid fully sealed | Division is fastest, as often as about every 20 minutes, only when nutrients are plentiful and the temperature suits the bacteria.
M3@3: Why is a Petri dish lid taped at a few points rather than sealed all the way round? | Oxygen can enter, so anaerobic pathogens are not encouraged | Air must flow in to wash away the condensation | Full sealing would let airborne microbes in faster | Sealed plates cannot be stored upside down at all | Tape keeps airborne microbes out, but a full seal would remove oxygen and favour harmful anaerobic bacteria.
M3@3: A hospital lab incubates cultures at 37 °C but a school uses 25 °C. Which is the best explanation? | Schools reduce the risk of growing human pathogens | Bacteria cannot grow at all above 25 °C | Hospitals want cultures to grow more slowly | Bacteria grow faster at 25 °C than at 37 °C | At 37 °C cultures grow faster, which suits hospitals, but schools keep to 25 °C or below so pathogens are less likely to grow.
SUM: Bacteria multiply by binary fission, and with enough nutrients and a suitable temperature they can divide as often as about every 20 minutes.
SUM: Tests of disinfectants, antiseptics and antibiotics need pure cultures, because contaminating microbes compete for nutrients and may be pathogens.
SUM: Dishes and agar are sterilised and the loop is flamed to kill unwanted microbes before the culture is made.
SUM: Lids are taped but not fully sealed, plates are stored upside down, and school cultures are incubated at 25 °C or below.

lessons.title: Calculating bacterial population growth
lessons.text:
## Calculating bacterial population growth
LV: GCSE
S: Because each bacterium splits in two, a population doubles every division time, so numbers rise very fast. Working out how many divisions happen, and writing huge answers in standard form, is a calculation examiners set often.
PRE: Culturing microorganisms
PRE: Scientific notation
O: Work out how many divisions take place from the time available and the mean division time
O: Calculate how many bacteria a population will contain after repeated doubling
O: Write a large bacterial population in standard form
REQ: aqa-gcse-biology:4.1.1.6.g @1,2
REQ: aqa-gcse-biology:4.1.1.6.h @3
T: Mean division time | The average time it takes for a bacterial population to double in number
T: Standard form | A way of writing a number as a value from 1 to less than 10 multiplied by a power of 10
H: Doubling, again and again
P: Every time the bacteria divide, each cell becomes two, so the population doubles. After one division there are twice as many, after two divisions four times as many, after three divisions eight times as many. After n divisions the population has been multiplied by 2^{n}.
E: number of bacteria at the end = number at the start × 2^{n} :: n is the number of divisions
E: n = time available ÷ mean division time :: use the same units for both times
D: bio-growth-curve
K: First find the number of divisions by dividing the time available by the mean division time, in the same units. Then multiply the starting number by 2 raised to that number.
!: Mixing units. If the division time is in minutes, change the total time into minutes before dividing: 6 hours is 360 minutes, not 6.
!: Multiplying by the number of divisions instead of doubling. Ten divisions multiply the population by 2^{10}, which is 1024, not by 10 or by 20.
H: Worked examples
X: One bacterium divides every 20 minutes. How many bacteria are there after 2 hours?
> Change the time to minutes: 2 hours is 120 minutes.
> Number of divisions: 120 ÷ 20 = 6
> The population doubles 6 times, and 2^{6} is 64.
> Starting from 1 bacterium, there are 64 bacteria.
X: Ten bacteria are placed in broth. The mean division time is 20 minutes. How many are there after 2 hours?
> Number of divisions: 120 ÷ 20 = 6, so the multiplier is 2^{6}, which is 64.
> Final number: 10 × 64 = 640
> In standard form, 640 is 6.4 × 10^{2}.
X: A single bacterium has a mean division time of 30 minutes. How many bacteria will there be after 8 hours? Give your answer in standard form to 3 significant figures.
> Change the time to minutes: 8 hours is 480 minutes.
> Number of divisions: 480 ÷ 30 = 16
> Final number is 2^{16}, which is 65536.
> To 3 significant figures that is 65500, which in standard form is 6.55 × 10^{4}.
H: Standard form for big populations
P: Bacterial numbers quickly reach hundreds of thousands, so answers are often written in standard form. Move the decimal point until the first part is between 1 and 10, and count the places moved to get the power of 10. For example, 1 bacterium dividing every 20 minutes for 6 hours makes 18 divisions and 2^{18}, which is 262144 bacteria: about 2.62 × 10^{5}.
!: Writing 26.2 × 10^{4}. It is the same size, but it is not standard form, because the first number must be at least 1 and less than 10.
H: Differences by tier
P: In AQA GCSE Biology, every triple-science student counts divisions and works out the final number. Giving the answer in standard form is a Higher tier skill.
Q: How do you find the number of divisions? | Divide the time available by the mean division time, using the same units for both.
Q: What is the formula for the final number of bacteria? | Final number = starting number × 2^{n}, where n is the number of divisions.
Q: What does mean division time mean? | The average time it takes the population to double in number.
Q: What is the commonest unit mistake in these calculations? | Not converting hours into minutes before dividing by a division time given in minutes.
Q: What range must the first number in standard form lie in? | At least 1 and less than 10.
M1@1: Bacteria divide every 20 minutes. How many divisions happen in 3 hours? | 9 | 3 | 6 | 60 | 3 hours is 180 minutes, and 180 divided by 20 gives 9 divisions.
NUM2@1,2: One bacterium divides every 20 minutes. How many bacteria are there after 3 hours? | 512 | 0 | bacteria | 3 hours is 180 minutes; 180 ÷ 20 = 9 divisions; 1 × 2^{9} = 512 bacteria.
M2@2: A culture starts with 100 bacteria and the mean division time is 30 minutes. How many are there after 4 hours? | 25600 | 800 | 1600 | 12800 | 4 hours is 240 minutes, giving 8 divisions; 2^{8} is 256, and 100 × 256 = 25600.
M2@3: Which shows 25600 in standard form? | 2.56 × 10^{4} | 25.6 × 10^{3} | 2.56 × 10^{3} | 256 × 10^{2} | The first number must be from 1 to less than 10, and the decimal point moves 4 places, so the power is 4.
M3@2,3: One bacterium divides every 20 minutes for 6 hours. Which answer is correct, in standard form to 3 significant figures? | 2.62 × 10^{5} | 3.60 × 10^{2} | 1.80 × 10^{1} | 2.62 × 10^{4} | 6 hours is 360 minutes, so there are 18 divisions; 2^{18} is 262144, which is about 2.62 × 10^{5}.
SA3@1,2,3: A single bacterium has a mean division time of 30 minutes. Calculate the number of bacteria after 8 hours and give the answer in standard form. | 8 hours is 480 minutes. Dividing by 30 gives 16 divisions. The population is 1 × 2^{16}, which is 65536 bacteria, about 6.55 × 10^{4} in standard form. | Converts 8 hours to 480 minutes ; Finds 16 divisions ; Uses 2^{16} to get 65536 ; Writes 6.55 × 10^{4}
SUM: The number of divisions is the time available divided by the mean division time, with both in the same units.
SUM: The final population is the starting number multiplied by 2 to the power of the number of divisions.
SUM: Large populations are written in standard form, with a first number from 1 to less than 10; at AQA this is a Higher tier skill.

lessons.title: Required practical: antiseptics, antibiotics and zones of inhibition
lessons.text:
## Required practical: antiseptics, antibiotics and zones of inhibition
LV: GCSE
S: Which antiseptic or antibiotic stops bacteria best? You can find out by placing soaked paper discs on a lawn of bacteria and measuring the clear zone around each one, then turning each zone into an area so the substances can be compared fairly.
PRE: Culturing microorganisms
O: Describe how to test antiseptics or antibiotics on a bacterial lawn, including a control
O: Calculate the area of a clear zone or a round colony from its diameter using πr²
O: Use zone areas to decide which substance or concentration is most effective
REQ: aqa-gcse-biology:4.1.1.6.RP2 @1,3
REQ: aqa-gcse-biology:4.1.1.6.f @2
T: Zone of inhibition | The clear area around a test substance where bacteria did not grow
T: Antiseptic | A substance put on living tissue or surfaces to kill germs or stop them growing
T: Antibiotic | A medicine that controls bacteria inside the body by killing them or stopping them reproducing
T: Control disc | A disc soaked in water or with no test substance, to show any clear zone is caused by the substance
H: The method
- Using aseptic technique, spread bacteria evenly over an agar plate with a sterile spreader to make a lawn.
- Soak filter-paper discs in different antiseptics or antibiotics, or in different concentrations of one substance.
- Place the discs on the agar, spaced apart, and add a **control disc** with no test substance.
- Tape the lid at a few points, label the plate, store it upside down and incubate at 25 °C.
- Measure the diameter of the clear zone around each disc.
DNEED: An agar plate with a bacterial lawn and four labelled filter-paper discs, three with clear zones of different sizes and a control disc with no zone, with one zone's diameter and radius marked
K: A clear zone means the substance killed the bacteria or stopped them reproducing. The bigger the zone, the more effective the substance against that bacterium.
!: Leaving out the control. Without a disc that has no test substance, you cannot show that the paper itself or handling did not cause the clear zone.
H: From diameter to area
P: Zones and colonies are roughly circular, so their size is compared as an area. You usually measure the diameter with a ruler, so halve it to get the radius r, then use the area of a circle.
E: area = πr^{2} :: r is the radius, half the diameter; units are mm^{2} if r is in mm
X: The clear zone around a disc has a diameter of 10 mm. Calculate its area, using 3.14 for π.
> Radius: 10 ÷ 2 = 5 mm
> r^{2} is 5 × 5 = 25 mm^{2}
> Area: 3.14 × 25 = 78.5 mm^{2}
X: Zone A has a diameter of 12 mm and zone B a diameter of 20 mm. How much larger is the area of zone B? Use 3.14 for π.
> Zone A radius: 12 ÷ 2 = 6 mm, so r^{2} is 36 and area is 3.14 × 36 = 113.04 mm^{2}
> Zone B radius: 20 ÷ 2 = 10 mm, so r^{2} is 100 and area is 3.14 × 100 = 314 mm^{2}
> Difference: 314 − 113.04 = 200.96 mm^{2}
> Zone B's substance was more effective against this bacterium.
!: Using the diameter in πr². Squaring the diameter instead of the radius makes the area four times too big. Always halve the diameter first.
!: Comparing zones by width alone. Convert each diameter to a radius and then to an area, so zones are compared fairly.
SAFE: Treat the cultures as possible pathogens: keep the lid taped while you measure the zones, follow your teacher's instructions and return plates for safe disposal.
Q: What does a clear zone around a disc show? | The substance killed the bacteria or stopped them reproducing in that area.
Q: Why is a control disc used? | To show that any clear zone is caused by the test substance, not the paper disc itself.
Q: What is the first step in finding a zone's area from its diameter? | Halve the diameter to get the radius.
Q: What is the formula for the area of a circular zone? | Area = πr^{2}, where r is the radius.
Q: What does a larger zone of inhibition mean? | The substance was more effective at killing or stopping the growth of that bacterium.
M1@1: Why is a disc with no test substance put on the plate? | It is a control, showing zones are caused by the substances | It feeds the bacteria so the lawn grows evenly | It keeps the lid from touching the agar surface | It soaks up condensation from the lid of the plate | A control disc shows that the paper disc alone does not produce a clear zone, so any zone comes from the substance.
M1@2: A clear zone has a diameter of 8 mm. What is its radius? | 4 mm | 8 mm | 16 mm | 64 mm | The radius is half the diameter, and 8 ÷ 2 = 4, so the radius is 4 mm.
M2@2: A zone has a diameter of 10 mm. Using 3.14 for π, what is its area? | 78.5 mm^{2} | 31.4 mm^{2} | 314 mm^{2} | 15.7 mm^{2} | Halve the diameter to get a 5 mm radius; 5 squared is 25, and 3.14 × 25 = 78.5 mm^{2}.
M2@3: Disc P has a zone of area 113 mm^{2} and disc Q a zone of 314 mm^{2}. What can you conclude? | Q's substance was more effective against these bacteria | P's substance was more effective against these bacteria | Both substances were equally effective on the bacteria | Neither substance had any effect on these bacteria | A larger clear zone means more bacteria were killed or stopped from reproducing, so the substance on disc Q worked better.
M3@2,3: A student squares the diameter of each zone and multiplies by 3.14. What effect does this have? | Every area is four times too big | Every area is twice too big | Every area is half the true value | The areas are correct for comparison | Using the diameter doubles r, and squaring doubles it again, so each area is four times the true value.
SA3@1,3: Describe how you would compare the effectiveness of three antiseptics on one type of bacterium. | Use aseptic technique to spread a lawn of the bacterium on an agar plate. Place filter-paper discs soaked in each antiseptic, plus a control disc, on the agar. Tape the lid at a few points, store upside down and incubate at 25 °C. Measure each clear zone's diameter, halve it, and calculate area with πr²; the largest area shows the most effective antiseptic. | Lawn using aseptic technique ; Soaked discs and a control ; Taped, inverted, incubated at 25 °C ; Measures zones and uses πr² ; Largest zone is most effective
SUM: To test antiseptics or antibiotics, soaked filter-paper discs and a control disc are placed on a bacterial lawn and the plate is incubated at 25 °C.
SUM: A clear zone shows where bacteria were killed or could not reproduce, and a larger zone means a more effective substance.
SUM: To find a zone's area, halve its diameter to get the radius and then use area = πr², with units of mm².
